# Disagree with the data, not the person

A team without conflict is not an aligned team, it is a team where someone gave up speaking. Disagreement is raw material for good decisions; what separates productive conflict from destructive is not intensity, it is the target. Productive conflict attacks premises, data, and interpretations. Destructive conflict attacks competence, intent, and person, and once the conversation crosses that line, no data brings it back.

The simplest technique is reframing the disagreement as a question about evidence. 'That will not work' closes the door and invites defense; 'what evidence would change your reading?' opens the path to a test. The second technique is separating position from interest: marketing's position may be 'we need the campaign in April' while the interest is 'hitting the half's goal', and it is in the interest that negotiation is possible, because campaigns are one among several ways to get there.

The third is declaring the disagreement early. Stored divergence does not evaporate: it reappears as lukewarm execution, passive sabotage, or that comment in the wrong meeting, in front of the wrong people.

[["Phrase that blocks","Phrase that unlocks","What changed"],["That will not work","What evidence would change your reading","Leaves opinion, goes to the test"],["You do not understand the client","Our data diverges, let us look together","Attacks the data, not the person"],["We already decided, move on","I disagree and commit, we measure in six weeks","Commitment with a set review"],["I am escalating this right now","We need a decision by Thursday, here are the options","Escalation with deadline and material"]]
Escalating is not accusing: it is bringing two honest readings to whoever has the authority to decide between them, with the other party knowing you are going up.

## Escalating well

Escalation has a bad name because it is almost always done badly. Done well, it is a service to the company: a stuck decision has a cost of delay, and someone must pay the bill to unstick it. The criterion of WHEN is objective: escalate when the decision is stalled, the parties have tried to resolve it at their own level, and waiting costs money or measurable opportunity. Escalating out of impatience, at the first divergence, spends credit you will want later.

The HOW is where most err. Tell the other party before going up, always, without exception; nobody forgives finding out behind their back. Bring both versions, yours and theirs, written so the other party would recognize their own position in your summary. Arrive with options and a recommendation, not with a complaint. And ask for a decision with a date, because escalation without a deadline merely moves the block one floor up.

After the decision comes the part that defines reputation: disagree and commit. You register the divergence once, agree on the milestone when the topic will be measured again, and execute with full energy. Lukewarm execution to prove you were right is the most expensive way of being right.

# A strategy nobody knows does not exist

The perfect document, approved by the board and kept in a folder, has zero impact. Strategy only becomes behavior when the people making a thousand small decisions a week can repeat it in their own words. Until support knows who the priority audience is, it will prioritize the queue by the client's tone of voice; until sales knows the noes, it will promise what does not exist.

Selling internally starts with narrative, and narrative has a fixed shape: what is happening, why it happens, what we chose, what it changes for you, and how we will know it worked. The first three parts are the same for everyone, because they are the diagnosis and the bet. The fourth changes per audience, and it is what makes the message stick: telling sales we do not promise business accounts this year is more useful than any vision slide. The fifth closes the honesty contract, because it gives everyone the right to charge for the promised outcome.

STRATEGY NARRATIVE (90 seconds, same base for everyone)

1. WHAT IS HAPPENING
   The base grows and does not retain: 18% D30 retention.

2. WHY IT HAPPENS
   The product solves once. The freelancer is the exception:
   their money decision comes back every week.

3. WHAT WE CHOSE
   Concentrate on the service freelancer's weekly cycle.
   We will not do business accounts nor credit this year.

4. WHAT CHANGES FOR YOU
   Sales       we do not promise business; the pitch becomes freelancers
   Support     the segment's queue gets priority
   Marketing   channel and message only for freelancers
   Engineering business accounts go into maintenance, no evolution

5. HOW WE WILL KNOW IT WORKED
   Segment D30 retention from 34% to 45% by June.

[["Moment","Narrative cut","Common mistake"],["Company-wide meeting","Diagnosis and bet in 90 seconds","Reading the whole document aloud"],["One-on-one with a peer","What changes in their work","Talking only about your team and goals"],["Executive committee","The bet, the risk, and the decision requested","Showing execution detail"],["New person arriving","The full story, with the noes","Handing over only the document link"]]
You will get sick of your own strategy long before the organization hears it for real the first time. Repeat it anyway.

## Repetition and allies

Two mechanics turn narrative into adoption. The first is repetition, and it is counterintuitive: the moment you cannot stand talking about the bet anymore, half the company is hearing it attentively for the first time. Internal communication is not an event, it is frequency; the same message, in the same terms, on different channels, for months. Changing the words at every presentation to avoid seeming repetitive destroys exactly the effect you want, which is the sentence becoming shared vocabulary.

The second is coalition. Strategy does not pass in the big meeting, it passes in small conversations before it. Identify the map's influencers, take the material to each one individually, hear the objections while they can still be incorporated, and arrive at the meeting with the room already partly convinced. That is not manipulation, it is respect for collective time: no good decision is born from the first exposure of a complex subject to ten people simultaneously.

The opposite has a name and a known cost: the influential area discovering the strategy along with everyone else, feeling run over, and becoming a permanent opponent, not over the content, but over the process. Recovering that relationship takes quarters. Avoiding it takes three half-hour conversations.

# Four variables, none for free

Every delivery negotiation moves four variables: scope (how much gets done), deadline (when it is ready), quality (how much is tested, documented, and supported) and people (how many participate). They are linked: moving one changes at least one other. The PM's role in the conversation is keeping that link from staying implicit, because when nobody declares the trade, it happens by itself, and the variable yielding in silence is always the same one, quality.

People deserve a separate warning. Intuition says doubling the team doubles speed, and reality says the opposite in the short term: new people consume whoever was already producing, in explanation, review, and coordination. Frederick Brooks summarized this decades ago and the lesson remains ignored every tight quarter. Adding people can help on long projects, with maturation time; on a late project needing to deliver in three weeks, it delays further.

The mature conversation, therefore, is not about effort or will. It is about which variable yields, who decides that, and what the company loses in each option.

[["Incoming request","Honest trade","Dishonest trade"],["Pull the date up three weeks","Cut two scope themes","Promising everything and cutting testing"],["Add a feature to the scope","Delay the date or swap another","Absorbing it with months of overtime"],["Double the team mid-project","Accept an early pace drop","Promising double the speed"],["Keep scope, deadline, team, and quality","None: some variable will yield","Letting quality yield quietly"]]
When nobody chooses which variable yields, quality yields alone, with no meeting and no minutes. It is the only one with nobody to defend it in the room.

## The constructive no

The no that works in scope negotiation is almost never the word 'no'. It is the trade placed on the table: 'I can deliver A and B by the agreed date, or A, B, and C three weeks later, and the choice is yours'. Notice what that sentence does: it refuses nothing, returns the decision to whoever holds authority over it, and makes the cost visible. The counterpart leaves with power, you leave with an executable plan, and nobody leaves deceived.

Three rules complete the practice. First, negotiate with numbers, not feelings: 'that is five weeks of two people' ends discussions that 'that is a lot of work' only prolongs. Second, never accept all four variables fixed at once, because accepting means taking alone a risk that belongs to the company; state the impossibility at the moment, politely, and propose the viable combinations. Third, record the agreement the same day, in short text, with what enters, what leaves, and the date; memory under negotiation pressure is notoriously creative three weeks later.

With the stakeholder map, managing up, productive conflict, and internal selling, you have the set that takes strategy out of the document. The final module brings it all together in a single case, from diagnosis to one-pager.

# Financem: initial traction and a fork

Financem is a fictional finance app, two years old, with that age's most common problem: enough traction to prove demand exists, not enough to prove a business exists. It has 40 thousand monthly active users, 6 thousand of them paying R$ 39 on the single plan, giving R$ 234 thousand of monthly recurring revenue. Paid acquisition grows 12% a month and the active base has been flat for two quarters, which already tells half the story.

The other half is retention. At D30, the general base retains 18%: four in five people vanish before the second month. Within it there is a group behaving differently. Service freelancers, about 8 thousand active, retain 34% and convert to paid at 30%, against a 15% average. They cost less to acquire, because they arrive by referral, and complain about specific things in support: taxes, lean months, the mixing of work and home money.

The board asked to double revenue in twelve months. Cash lasts fourteen. The team has nine people.

[["Indicator","Current value","Reading"],["Monthly active base","40,000 users","Flat for two quarters, despite acquisition"],["Payers","6,000 on the R$ 39 plan","Recurring revenue of R$ 234,000 a month"],["General D30 retention","18%","Four in five vanish in the first month"],["Freelancer D30 retention","34%","Almost double the base average"],["Freelancer conversion","30% against a 15% average","The segment pays at double the rate"],["Cash and team","14 months and 9 people","One wrong bet consumes half the runway"]]

THE THREE PATHS ON THE TABLE

A. GO DEEP ON THE SERVICE FREELANCER
   Addressable market: about 1.2 million people
   Needed team: the current one, 9 people
   Evidence for: 34% retention and 30% conversion
   Risk: smaller revenue ceiling on a 3-year horizon

B. OPEN A BUSINESS VERSION FOR MICRO-COMPANIES
   Addressable market: about 4.5 million companies
   Possible price: R$ 149/month against R$ 39 today
   Entry cost: 2 quarters of invoicing and
   reconciliation, plus 1 person dedicated to compliance
   Risk: long sales cycle and a team split in two

C. CREDIT BASED ON CASH FLOW
   Potential revenue: the largest of the three
   Prerequisites: capital, a banking partner, and
   regulatory authorization (estimated 9 to 12 months)
   Risk: scaling a product that does not yet retain
Acquisition rising 12% a month with a flat active base is not a marketing problem: it is a receipt that the bucket leaks as fast as it fills.

## What the board asked and what cash allows

Doubling revenue in twelve months means going from R$ 234 thousand to R$ 468 thousand a month. There are only three levers for that: more payers, a bigger price, or fewer people leaving. The cash constraint changes the weight of each. With fourteen months of runway, any path only starting to return money in the twelfth month is an all-or-nothing bet, and all-or-nothing bets at a company that has not found retention are usually the last decision the company makes.

Notice also what the numbers do NOT say. They do not say the freelancer is the world's best market, nor that business is bad; business has a bigger market and a price almost four times the current one, which is serious. They say Financem has a leak in the base and a group that does not leak, and that two of the three paths spend quarters before touching that leak.

# The central challenge in three sentences

The diagnosis must explain WHY performance is what it is, not repeat that it is bad. The document's version says: Financem solves a problem once, because after the first organized month it returns no new value; the exception is the service freelancer, whose money decision repeats every week, and that is why they retain 34% against 18% and convert 30% against 15%; the bottleneck, therefore, is not the funnel's top, it is the absence of a weekly reason to return.

Apply the first module's prohibition test: does this diagnosis forbid anything? It does. It forbids buying more traffic while the bucket leaks, which already knocks down the most obvious move facing the board's goal. It also forbids treating retention as an interface problem, because the reading is not 'the product is confusing', it is 'the product has no reason to be opened on a Tuesday morning'.

From the reading, the guiding policy comes out almost by itself: concentrate the whole product on the service freelancer's weekly cash cycle, until being the obvious choice for this audience. A general approach, not a feature, exactly as Rumelt describes.

DIAGNOSIS, BET, AND THE TWO NOES

CENTRAL CHALLENGE
Financem solves a problem once: after the first organized
month, it returns no new value. The exception is the
service freelancer, whose money decision repeats every
week (34% retention against 18%, 30% conversion against
15%). The bottleneck is not the funnel's top, it is the
absence of a weekly reason to return.

GUIDING POLICY
Concentrate the whole product on the service freelancer's
weekly cash cycle, until we are their obvious choice.

THE TWO NOES OF THIS YEAR
NO: business version. Consumes 2 quarters on invoicing and
    compliance and does not touch the retention bottleneck.
    Revisit set: October.
NO: credit. Depends on capital and a license (9 to 12 months)
    and scales a product that does not yet retain.
    Revisit set: when D30 retention passes 45%.

A no without a date is a cowardly maybe. Writing when the topic returns to the table costs one line and keeps it from returning every week.

## Why the noes need dates

The document's two noes do not say business and credit are bad ideas. They say they are not THIS year's game, with THIS team and THIS cash, and each carries the condition that would reopen the discussion: business returns in October, with segment saturation data; credit returns when D30 retention passes 45%, because lending money on top of a product people abandon amplifies a problem instead of solving it.

This way of refusing does three jobs at once. It protects focus, because the request does not return next week in different clothes. It protects the relationship, because whoever defended business leaves the meeting with a date, not a closed door. And it protects the strategy itself against stubbornness, because the revisit condition is also the trigger forcing the team to look again, even if the bet is going well.

Module 1's final test is satisfied: someone important complains. Sales loses business contracts already in this year's funnel, and that loss is the most reliable evidence that a real choice was made. A strategy approved with nobody displeased is almost always a wish list with a new cover.

# One objective, three results

The bet is written and now must touch the quarter. The cycle's objective translates the guiding policy into a sentence the team repeats in the hallway: make the service freelancer come back every week because Financem decides WITH them, not just records what already happened. Qualitative, time-bound, and aligned with the diagnosis without naming any solution.

The three KRs measure outcome in layers that explain each other. Segment D30 retention, from 34% to 45%, is the number proving the central thesis: if weekly value exists, people stay. Weekly usage, defined as three active weeks out of four, from 21% to 35%, measures the habit producing retention and reacts before it, giving a progress reading mid-cycle. Conversion to paid in the segment, from 30% to 38%, links habit to the revenue the board demands.

Two guardrail metrics keep the number from rising for the wrong reason: the segment's NPS must not fall below 45, and support's response time stays under six hours.

QUARTER'S OKR (April to June)

OBJECTIVE
Make the service freelancer come back every week because
Financem decides with them, not just records the past.

KR1  Segment D30 retention:           from 34% to 45%
KR2  Weekly usage (3 weeks in 4):      from 21% to 35%
KR3  Conversion to paid in segment:    from 30% to 38%

GUARDRAIL METRICS (must not worsen)
- Segment NPS does not fall below 45 (today 48)
- Support response time stays under 6 hours

INITIATIVES (hypotheses, outside the OKR, swappable along the way)
- Weekly cash summary with one suggested decision
- Automatic tax reserve in onboarding
- Atypical week alert on the preferred channel

AGREED RULER
Targets are stretch: 70% of each KR is declared success.
Agreed on day 1, not on day 90.

[["Key Result","Part of the bet it proves","Baseline and target"],["Segment D30 retention","That weekly value holds the user","34% to 45%"],["Weekly usage, 3 of 4 weeks","That there is habit, not just install","21% to 35%"],["Conversion to paid","That habit becomes revenue in the cycle","30% to 38%"],["Segment NPS, guardrail","That habit did not come from nagging","48 today, floor of 45"]]
Three layered KRs tell one story: habit happens, retention responds, revenue follows. If the first layer does not move, the thesis fell early.

## What stayed out, and why

Three candidates were refused when writing the OKR, and the refusals teach more than the accepted ones. 'Launch the weekly cash summary' stayed out because it is delivery: the team can launch it and the user may still not return. It lives on the initiatives list, where it can be swapped mid-cycle without anyone touching the KRs.

'Double the company's revenue' stayed out because the team does not control the variable within a quarter: half of it depends on price, channel, and market. The OKR takes the piece this team moves now, and the chain to the board's goal is explicit in the document, not inside the KR.

'Run 20 interviews with freelancers' stayed out because it is activity. Interviewing is a means, and an important one; the honest KR is what the interviews should cause. Notice the healthy side effect of these three refusals: they return freedom to the team. With outcome KRs, if in week six the weekly summary does not move usage, nobody needs permission to switch initiatives, because the commitment taken was to the user's number, not to Monday's plan.

# Themes by horizon, commitment per item

Financem's roadmap organizes the bet into three horizons of uncertainty and declares, item by item, the level of commitment taken. In NOW sit two themes of different natures, and that is deliberate. The first is 'a weekly reason to return', the bet's heart, with a success measure tied to the weekly usage KR and WINDOW level: second quarter, revised on the first Monday of each month. The second is compliance with the freelancer's new payment-book rule, which takes effect on July 1 and is therefore a COMMITMENT with a firm date, the plan's only one.

In NEXT sits the lean-month forecast, still in discovery, with a test set for May with 40 users. BET level: no dates until the test speaks. Beside it, the split between personal and work spending, chosen because it feeds the forecast.

In LATER sit the year's two noes with their reopening conditions written: the relationship with the accountant, which depends on NEXT's result, and cash-flow credit, which requires a license and a base that retains.

  Level: COMMITMENT, external obligation with a firm date

NEXT (likely direction)

  Level: BET, window defined after the test
- Theme: personal vs work spending split
  Why: it feeds the lean-month forecast

A roadmap with a single date commitment and the rest declared as window or bet is not vague: it is the most honest the team can be.

## The executive version in five minutes

The executive cut is the table above, plus three risk lines and one requested decision. No scope, no point estimates, no screen names. The reading the director needs in five minutes is this: there are two themes in execution, one of them with a firm date because the law says so, the rest is declared as bets with learning milestones, and the number that will say whether the strategy works is the segment's weekly usage.

The sales cut starts from the same document and cuts more: value themes in the client's language, only the July date, which is a real commitment, and no mention of the LATER bets. The team's cut expands in the opposite direction, with the evidence behind each theme, the success measure, and the scope boundaries.

Three zooms, one source. When the May test returns a result, the change appears in all three cuts the same week, with the same why recorded in one line: date, move, reason. It is that record, not the drawing of the columns, that keeps the roadmap alive after the third month.

# The whole strategy on one page

The previous four lessons produced loose pieces. This one joins them in the format the trail has been building since the first module: one page with diagnosis, bet, OKRs, roadmap, and risks. The size constraint is not aesthetic. Five sections on one page force every sentence to work, and it is precisely the impossibility of padding that exposes the choices not made.

An outside reader should be able to answer five questions in five minutes: what is the central challenge, what is the bet, what stayed out, how we will know it is working, and what would topple the plan. If any of them requires an explanation meeting, the document is not ready yet.

Notice, reading the board below, the stitching between sections. The diagnosis names the absence of weekly value; the bet picks the freelancer's weekly cycle; the main KR measures weekly usage; the NOW theme is called a weekly reason to return; the declared risk is precisely the premise that weekly value moves retention. The same idea runs through the five sections, and that is the practical definition of coherence.

FINANCEM: PRODUCT STRATEGY (one page, review 04/05)

1. DIAGNOSIS
The product solves once and returns no new value: D30
retention of 18%. The service freelancer is the exception
(34% retention, 30% conversion) because their decision
repeats every week. The bottleneck is the absence of a
weekly reason.

2. BET (guiding policy)
Concentrate the product on the service freelancer's weekly
cash cycle until we are this audience's obvious choice.
NOT this year: business version (revisit in October) and
credit (revisit when D30 retention passes 45%).

3. QUARTER'S OKR
Objective: make the freelancer come back every week because
Financem decides with them.
KR1 Segment D30 retention:        34% to 45%
KR2 Weekly usage (3 of 4 weeks):  21% to 35%
KR3 Conversion to paid:           30% to 38%
Guardrail: segment NPS not below 45.

4. ROADMAP
NOW   weekly reason (second-quarter window); payment-book
      rule (commitment, firm date of July 1)
NEXT  lean-month forecast (test with 40 users in May)
LATER accountant; cash-flow credit

5. RISKS AND ASSUMPTIONS
Assumption: weekly value moves retention. Falls if the May
test lands below 30% weekly usage.
Risk: losing the business window in 2026. Mitigation:
October revisit with the segment's saturation data.
Risk: dependence on a single segment. Mitigation: measure
the niche's organic growth ceiling monthly.

A good strategy document is not the one that convinces in the presentation: it is the one still answering questions when you are not in the room to defend it.

## What this document proves

A one-pager like this is an uncommon portfolio piece, because it shows reasoning instead of a pretty screen. Whoever reads it can see how you read numbers (acquisition rising with a flat base), how you choose (the segment already retaining, against two bigger markets), how you refuse (with a revisit condition, not a closed door), how you measure (layered outcomes, with a guardrail), and how you communicate uncertainty (one date commitment, the rest declared as window or bet).

Redoing the exercise with a real product, yours or one from a company you know from outside, is the natural next step. The data will be worse and messier than Financem's, and that is exactly where the technique proves itself: writing the central challenge with incomplete information, betting while bearing the cost of the noes, and declaring the premise that, if it falls, topples the whole plan.

From diagnosis to influence, this trail's journey was a single argument: strategy is the sum of choices someone signed, measured by numbers nobody doctored, and communicated until they become shared vocabulary. The document is only the place where those three things are visible at once, and revisable when reality changes.
